summary: Defines a set of structured header fields that mailing list software can add to messages, using URLs to describe list commands such as subscribe and unsubscribe. This lets mail clients offer automated tools for list functions.

plainLanguage.summary: Little notes on each email from a mailing list that tell your mail program how to join or leave, so it can show buttons.

questions: how do email clients unsubscribe from lists
what are the list-id style mailing list headers
subtitle: Standard List-* header fields that let mail programs show Subscribe, Unsubscribe and Help buttons for any mailing list.

tldr.problem: Every mailing list manager had its own cryptic commands for joining, leaving and getting help, so mail clients could not offer a common interface for them.
tldr.mechanism: List software adds structured header fields such as List-Help, List-Subscribe and List-Unsubscribe to each message. Each holds one or more angle-bracketed URLs, usually mailto, that locate the information or perform the command.
tldr.outcome: A mail client can read these fields and offer menu items or buttons for list functions, without knowing the list manager's own command syntax.

facts.label: Copies per message
facts.value: No more than one of each field

today: RFC 2369 is a Proposed Standard published in July 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why List Headers Exist
sections.content:
RFC 2369 defines a set of structured header fields to be added to email messages sent by email distribution lists. Each field typically contains a URL, usually mailto (defined in RFC 2368), that locates the relevant information or performs the command directly.

The goal is to let mail clients provide automated tools for list functions, such as a menu item or push button. The intent stated in the RFC is to give a common interface to the often cryptic and varied mailing list manager commands.

Implementing the fields is optional. A list manager may choose to implement only one or two of them. Using them does not remove the requirement to support the -Request command address for mailing lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Every club has its own odd way to sign up or quit. These notes give every club the same kind of sign-up and quit button.

sections.title: Command Syntax and URL Lists
sections.content:
The fields follow the encoding rules for mail headers in RFC 822, and the URL content is further limited to URL-safe characters. The content mostly consists of URLs enclosed in angle brackets, < and >. MTAs MUST NOT insert whitespace inside the brackets, and clients should ignore any whitespace that badly behaved MTAs add.

A field may hold several alternate URLs, separated by commas. They are in order of preference from left to right. The client should use the leftmost protocol it supports, and should use another URL only if the first one failed. This lets a list offer an http link while still giving a mailto fallback for users who only have email.

Commands that need variable fields filled in by the client, such as the user's own address, are not supported. Such lists should still provide List-Help, perhaps pointing to a structured interface such as an HTML form.

For future extension, clients follow three rules. A field that does not begin with < (after whitespace and comments) SHOULD be ignored. Characters after a bracketed URL SHOULD be ignored unless a comma comes first. If a comma-separated item is not a bracketed URL, that item and all later ones SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note is an address in pointy brackets. If there are several, try the first one you understand, and only try the next if that one fails.

sections.title: The Six List Header Fields
sections.content:
The fields a list uses SHOULD appear on all messages the list distributes, including command responses to individual users, and on other messages that clearly apply to one distinct list. There MUST be no more than one of each field in a message. They MUST only be generated by mailing lists, not by end users.

  • List-Help is the most important. It points to complete instructions for the other commands, such as a help file or an instructive website. A list could include only this field.
  • List-Unsubscribe describes the command, preferably by mail, that removes the user from the list.
  • List-Subscribe describes the command that requests addition to the list.
  • List-Post describes how to post to the list. It is typically the list address but MAY be a moderator. For a list that does not allow posting, it may hold the special value NO.
  • List-Owner gives a path to contact a human administrator. It need not be given if that person is the postmaster.
  • List-Archive describes how to access the list archives.

List-Help, List-Subscribe and List-Unsubscribe are the three core fields. List-Post, List-Owner and List-Archive are less widely applicable but useful to enough lists to be formalized.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six kinds of notes: help, join, leave, post a message, contact the boss, and see old messages. A list can include as many or as few as it likes.

sections.title: Examples and Nested Lists
sections.content:
The RFC gives many examples. A unsubscribe field with a web link first and a mail fallback looks like the first example below, and a list that does not allow posting uses NO.

A list that is a sublist of another list in a nested hierarchy must adjust some fields. Sublists SHOULD remove the parent list's List-Help, List-Subscribe, List-Unsubscribe and List-Owner fields and insert their own. If the sublist has its own archive, it SHOULD replace List-Archive; otherwise it MUST leave that field untouched. Whether to replace List-Post depends on how postings are handled, and is left to the list managers.
sections.plainLanguage: A small group inside a bigger group should put up its own signs for joining and leaving, but can keep pointing to the big group's old messages if it has none of its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says there are very few new security concerns, since message headers are an existing standard designed to accommodate new types. Forged or duplicated headers are problems inherent in Internet email.

Mail list processors should not let user-originated list header fields pass through to their lists. On the client side, the user must be given a chance to confirm any action before it is executed. For mailto, a client may create the correctly formatted message without sending it so the user can approve or discard it.

All security considerations for URLs apply. Clients should not support list header URLs that could compromise the user's system, including file:// URLs, which could be used to trigger a local application on some systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Before your mail program sends a leave request for you, it should ask you first. It should also never follow a note that could make your computer run something it should not.

sections.title: Design Choices and Client Hints
sections.content:
The appendix records why the design is shaped this way. Several fields were chosen over one big field because a new meta-syntax would be harder to implement, long fields risk being modified by servers en route, and clients can implement each command independently. URLs were chosen over parameter lists because clients already parse URLs; the authors say this let them add prototype support to existing Macintosh mail clients, Eudora and Emailer, without changing their source code.

Variable substitution was rejected as too complicated, and a standard command language was set aside because of multilingual and custom needs and slow expected adoption. A specialized MIME part was considered but most clients did not support MIME well enough.

For clients, the RFC suggests key combinations, a menu of items such as Subscribe, Unsubscribe and Get Help, or push buttons. If a dialog is used, the client MUST offer the user a way to review, and possibly modify, the message before it is sent. If the user has several addresses, the client should ask which to use when subscribing, and should use the subscribed address when unsubscribing.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors picked web-style addresses because computers already know how to read them. They also said programs should always let you look at a request before it goes out.

items.label: Help
items.desc: Points to complete instructions for the list.

items.label: Join
items.desc: Command to request addition to the list.

items.label: Leave
items.desc: Command to be removed from the list.

items.label: Post
items.desc: How to post to the list; may be NO.

items.label: Owner
items.desc: How to contact a human administrator.

items.label: Archive
items.desc: How to access the list archives.

data.title: List header examples
data.code:
List-Unsubscribe: <http://www.host.com/list.cgi?cmd=unsub&lst=list>,
    <mailto:list-request@host.com?subject=unsubscribe>
List-Post: <mailto:list@host.com>
List-Post: NO (posting not allowed on this list)
List-Archive: <http://www.host.com/list/archive/> (Web Archive)
